4.text: The White River Group, numbering about 25 camps; and the group in the Peˊqul-ñei Mountains,

6.text: On the so-called Chukchee Peninsula, between Kuluˊči Bay, Holy Cross Bay, and the Pacific Ocean,

7.text: the whole number of reindeer-camps is from about 80 to 100. The herds are not very large,

8.text: owing to the severity of the climate and to scanty pasturage. Almost half of these camps

9.text: obtain the best part of their food from the sea; they keep dog-teams, own skin boats, etc.

10.text: Within the last thirty years the breeding of reindeer has increased grad-

11.text: ually, and even some of the Eskimo have succeeded in gathering herds of

12.text: their own; but the winter of 1900-01, when we were in the field, was so

13.text: unfavorable, that the reindeer were famished everywhere, and many of the

14.text: northern herdsmen especially lost about one-half of their whole stock.

15.text: It would be easy to increase the number of the divisions, since almost

16.text: every small cluster of camps, united by ties of kinship, claim to have a

17.text: separate name derived from the river on the banks of which they wander

18.text: with their herds. Thus Mr. Bogdanovitch gives the name Tahrait to those

19.text: living around St. Lawrence Bay near the river Marich. Perhaps this is a

20.text: distorted form of the word teg̣reˊtɪlɪt (“those coming down [the river]”).

21.text: According to the situation of their districts in the western or the eastern

22.text: part of the country, the divisions of the Reindeer Chukchee call each other

23.text: eig̣ɪˊs˙qɪlɪt (“westerners;” literally, “those coming leeward”) or aivaˊʟaᵋt (“east-

24.text: erners;” literally, “those coming windward”). These names have arisen from

25.text: the fact that the chief wind of the country comes from the west along the

26.text: Arctic shore. Perhaps the names Aiˊwan and Eiwhueˊn have a common origin

27.text: with aivaˊʟat (from aiˊg̣-êpu, “windward”), since the inhabitants of the Pacific

28.text: coast are called Aivaˊʟat by all the inland and Arctic Chukchee, whom they,

29.text: in their turn, call indiscriminately Eig̣ɪˊs˙qɪlɪt.

30.text: All camps to the southeast from Chaun Bay are called by the more

31.text: eastern people Uˊnmɪ-nuteˊkinet (“those from the inland country”).²

32.text: The whole number of reindeer camps amounts to about 650, with a

33.text: population of 7500-9000, rather more than less.

34.text: In compiling the list of the maritime villages, I have utilized, besides

35.text: information collected by myself, the very valuable paper by Nordquist and the

36.text: official “Register of the Inhabited Places of the Seacoast Province of Siberia.”

37.text: In the latter the data relating to the Chukchee were furnished by Mr. N.

38.text: Gondatti. Unfortunately, while writing this memoir, I have not been able to

39.text: use the very valuable article of Mr. Gondatti, the title of which is given on

40.text: p. 20, but, so far as I can remember, it does not differ much from the Register.
